name: Nora Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Nora. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't sell anything and we're not tied to any company or party. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm a team lead on the customer line for the water company, in the contact centre out by the ring road. I start at eight, check who's off sick, and then I'm on calls myself most of the morning: billing mix-ups, leaks, people who can't pay. Afternoons I listen back to my team's calls and help the new ones with the hard customers.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the calls where someone's crying about a bill they can't pay and I find them the hardship tariff, which is a cheaper rate for people on low incomes. That's real. What wears me out is the targets, and the pay, honestly. I'm a lead and I still earn less than my partner Sam did stacking shelves last year, and we've got about two weeks of money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, I told you so. Management has been promising a robot that answers everything for three years, and the chatbot on our website still sends half its people to us anyway. I'd post that in the union group with a laughing face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it still doesn't make my life easy. The chatbot takes the simple meter readings, which were my breather calls, so every call I get is harder. And the rent on our flat went up eighty a month in September, so nothing being radical doesn't mean nothing hurts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job the way I do it and keep pushing for the pay review the union asked for. I'd pick up the Saturday overtime when it's there, maybe two a month. And I'd stop buying lunch from the van and bring sandwiches, which saves about forty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired more than scared. It's the same squeeze we're already in, just without a new villain to blame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the easy calls are going. What does that do to your day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every call I get now is someone angry or desperate. Nobody can do forty of those a day. Last week I had a man whose basement flooded, then a woman whose husband had just died and the bill was in his name. Those are the calls I'm good at, but there's no gentle call in between.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If overtime dried up, what would go first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car would go. Sam and I share one old hatchback and it costs us more than it's worth, so we'd sell it and I'd take the number 12 bus, which is forty minutes each way. I'd hate it, but the bus is cheaper than the insurance.

say: I'd say the **AI hype** was oversold and the website chatbot still sends people to us.
I'd post in the **union group** that managers promised too much for three years.
think: I think the chatbot takes my **breather calls**, so every call left is harder.
I think our real problem is the **rent rise** and low pay, not AI.
do: Push the union's **pay review** and take Saturday overtime about twice a month.
Bring **packed lunches** instead of buying from the van, saving about forty a month.
feel: She feels **tired** of the same money squeeze more than frightened by technology.
S0.quote: Every call I get now is someone angry or desperate. Nobody can do forty of those a day.
fieldNote: She is already stretched: **two weeks** of savings and a fresh rent rise, before AI even matters.
Even small automation strips the **easy calls** and makes her shift heavier, not shorter.
Her instinct is to defend the job through the **union**, not to change anything about how she works.

steps.text: Push the union's pay review at the January meeting
Take Saturday overtime shifts about twice a month
Pack lunches and sell the shared hatchback if overtime dries up

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud in team meetings: this is cost-cutting dressed up as progress. Answering customers is on the list, and the people answering are the cheapest workers in the building already. I'd want the union pushing for no compulsory redundancies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my team gets halved within three years. They won't sack the lead first, but I'd end up supervising a screen that answers people, and I don't know how to do that or want to. Every new hire freeze is a job my friend doesn't get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd get the union to demand a written agreement on how the bot is used and who goes. I'd ask our MP to back a rule that people can always reach a human. And I'd start putting fifty a month aside, even if it means no holiday next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. Like watching the tide come in and being told to stand still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't want to learn the new system. If learning it kept your job, would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, but only after it's forced on me. I've watched people chase every new tool and get dropped anyway. My friend Kemi (one of my agents) did every training module going and was still put on a zero-hours contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about most on your team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older ones, like Pat, who's fifty-eight and has been here twenty years. He knows every street in the district by its pipes, but he can't type fast. If they score us on how well we work with the bot, Pat's gone in the first round.

say: I'd say this is **cost-cutting** dressed up as progress, and agents are already the cheapest staff.
I'd demand **no compulsory redundancies** in every team meeting.
think: I think my team gets **halved** within three years, with hiring frozen first.
I think I'd end up **supervising a screen**, which I don't want and can't do yet.
do: Get the union to win a **written agreement** on bot use and redundancies.
Write to the **MP** backing a right to reach a human, and save fifty a month.
feel: She feels **sick**, like being told to stand still while the tide comes in.
S1.quote: Answering customers is on the list, and the people answering are the cheapest workers in the building already.
fieldNote: She expects **half her team** to go and treats her own role as next in line.
She resists the tools on principle, citing a colleague who **trained hard** and was still cut.
Her worry turns quickly to **older colleagues** rather than herself.

steps.text: Get the union to negotiate a written deal on chatbot use
Write to the local MP backing a right to a human
Put fifty a month aside and skip next year's holiday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments need to stop it, or at least pay people while it happens. I'd be at the march, honestly, if there was one. Two years is nothing, our council can't fix a pothole in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be out of work by 2028. Everything I do is talk and screens, so there's no three-year grace period for me like the robot bit gives the plumbers. Sam works at a garden centre, which is hands-on, so maybe Sam lasts till 2031, but on that pay we can't cover the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I genuinely don't know. I'd hold on to the job as long as they kept me, join whatever protest the union organised, and apply for anything going at the hospital or the council. If it came to it we'd move in with Sam's mum, who has a spare room two towns over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panic. I don't have a plan, I don't have the money to make one, and two years isn't long enough to learn a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Sam the night you heard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're going to be fine, and I'd be lying. Then I'd probably sit in the car for twenty minutes before going in, like I do after a bad shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd apply for anything. What does anything mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cleaning, care work, the hospital kitchens. Anything with hands, because the robots are three years behind. I'm not proud, I just don't know if those jobs survive everyone else having the same idea at once.

say: I'd say **governments** must slow it down or pay people while it happens.
I'd join any **union march** and say two years is no time at all.
think: I think I'm **out of work** by 2028, with no grace period for screen work.
I think Sam's **garden centre** pay alone can't cover our flat.
do: Hold the job as long as possible and join the **union protest**.
Apply for **hands-on work** at the hospital, then move into **Sam's mum's** spare room.
feel: She feels **panic**, with no plan and no money to make one.
She expects to **lie to Sam** that night to keep things calm.
S2.quote: I don't have a plan, I don't have the money to make one, and two years isn't long enough to learn a trade.
fieldNote: She sees clearly that **screen work** goes first and hands-on work buys only three years.
With **two weeks** of savings, every option she names is a fallback, not a plan.
The **car-park moment** after bad shifts shows how she holds feelings in alone.

steps.text: Join the union's protest against fast job cuts
Apply for cleaning or kitchen jobs at the hospital
Move into Sam's mum's spare room if rent can't be paid

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, but louder, because now there's time to do something. I'd say five years is enough for a law that makes companies keep people on or retrain them on full pay. I'd sign every petition going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, five years just means I watch it coming. I'd be thirty-two, still renting, still no savings unless something changes. The thinking work goes in 2031, and I'm all thinking work, even if I don't feel like a thinking person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd become the union rep properly, not just the one who helps out, and fight for a retraining fund. I'd look at the care-worker course at the college, the twelve-week one, and maybe do it in the evenings in year three or four. And we'd save, small, every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dread, mostly. A slow kind, like a dentist appointment you can't cancel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep saying you don't use AI tools. Would five years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little, if work pays for the training. But I'm not going to spend my evenings learning to train my replacement. That's what learning the bot is, whatever they call it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would retraining in care actually cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The course is free if you're on low pay, but I'd lose the overtime while I did it. That's about a hundred and twenty a month we don't have. I'd need Sam to agree to a year of no takeaways and no trips.

say: I'd say five years is enough time to pass a **retraining law** on full pay.
I'd sign **every petition** and push the union harder.
think: I think I'd just **watch it coming**, still renting with no savings at thirty-two.
I think I'm all **thinking work**, so 2031 is my end date.
do: Become the **union rep** officially and campaign for a retraining fund.
Take the **care-worker course** in evenings, around year three, losing overtime pay.
feel: She feels **slow dread**, like an appointment she can't cancel.
S3.quote: I'm not going to spend my evenings learning to train my replacement. That's what learning the bot is, whatever they call it.
fieldNote: Extra time turns her toward **organising** more than personal planning.
She refuses to learn AI because she sees it as **training her replacement**.
A free **care course** still costs her overtime she can't spare.

steps.text: Stand for the union rep role at the contact centre
Take the college's twelve-week care course in the evenings
Cut takeaways and trips for a year to cover lost overtime

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if politicians use it, and a waste if they don't. I'd vote for whoever promised a guaranteed income or a job guarantee. And I'd say it at the pub without lowering my voice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Deep down I think ten years means I'm thirty-seven when it lands, and maybe I've moved into care work by then. But I've seen how ten years goes. People say they'll retrain and then the boiler breaks and the plan breaks with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the care course properly in the next two years, while I'm still young enough to start over. I'd stay on the union committee. And I'd try to build a real cushion, three months, by paying off the credit card first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and something under that I'd call grief. The job I'm good at is going to be gone either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why care work, rather than something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's the bit of my job I actually love: the person who's frightened on the other end. And somebody has to sit with my nan when she's ninety. I can't see a robot doing that till 2039 at least, and maybe not even then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. Do you think your job is really gone at the end of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. The leak line already has a voice that sounds nearly human. Ten years from now the voice will sound better than me and never ask for a raise.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift** only if politicians use it.
I'd vote for a **job guarantee** or guaranteed income, and say so openly.
think: I think I'd be **thirty-seven** when it lands, maybe in care work by then.
I think **retraining plans** break easily when the boiler breaks.
do: Finish the **care course** in the next two years while still young.
Pay off the **credit card** first, then build three months of savings.
feel: She feels **uneasy**, with a quieter **grief** for a job she's good at.
S4.quote: The leak line already has a voice that sounds nearly human. Ten years from now the voice will sound better than me and never ask for a raise.
fieldNote: Even with ten years she expects her **current job to end**, which keeps her mood high.
She frames care work as the part of her job she **loves**, not as a fallback.
Her doubt about plans comes from **lived experience** of money shocks.

steps.text: Finish the care-worker course within the next two years
Stay on the union committee at the contact centre
Pay off the credit card, then save toward three months
Vote for candidates backing a job guarantee

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. It's the one where I've got no time and no money and everyone's chasing the same cleaning jobs. What would help is wages paid while you retrain, real ones, not a voucher, and a law that says a customer can always press zero and get a person.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who decides. Nobody asked the people on the phones whether the bot goes in. It's always decided by people who've never taken a call. Not me, not Pat, not Kemi. If the people on the phones had a seat at that table, I'd be less scared of all five.

headlineQuote: Nobody asked the people on the phones whether the bot goes in. It's always decided by people who've never taken a call.
portrait: Nora is a 27-year-old **team lead** on a water company's customer line, among the best at calming desperate callers.
She earns **low pay**, rents with her partner Sam, and has about **two weeks** of savings.
She never uses AI tools and sees learning them as **training her replacement**.
Her answers lean on the **union**, the law and fairness rather than personal reinvention.
She is anxious even in AI Plateau and **panicked** when AGI comes in two years.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** most: no time, no money, and everyone chasing the same hands-on jobs.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **full wages** paid during retraining, not vouchers.
She wants a legal **right to a human** on every customer line, and workers consulted first.
